title: Vayelech: strong and of good courage (Deuteronomy 31:7)
hook: Moses encourages Joshua in front of all Israel

segments.voice: Yesterday, vayelech: Moses went out to the people. Your line was he went to them. Who did you go to? Today, what he says to the man who will take his place. Day five hundred twenty-three.

Encouragement is often quiet. A text before an interview. A hand on the shoulder in a hallway. A quiet good luck at the door. Private encouragement is real, and good. But there's another kind that's harder to give: saying it out loud, in front of everyone, so the person hears it and so does everyone around them. It costs the speaker something. It puts their own name behind someone else. Moses chooses that kind.
screen: `A TEXT BEFORE THE INTERVIEW.` → `A HAND ON THE SHOULDER.` → `OR: OUT LOUD, IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: "And Moses called unto Joshua, and said unto him in the sight of all Israel: 'Be strong and of good courage.'" In Hebrew, chazak ve'ematz. Two words that overlap: be strong, be firm. Moses had already said the same words to the whole people a few verses earlier. Now he says them to one man, in front of everyone. Consider Joshua's position. He's following Moses, the one who spoke with God. Someone in his place might well wonder whether he could measure up, and whether the people would follow. A public blessing answers both doubts at once. Joshua hears that his teacher believes in him. And the people hear it too, so they know their new leader didn't grab the role. It was handed to him, with confidence, in daylight. The words keep traveling. Later in this chapter God says them to Joshua directly, and again, more than once, at the opening of the book of Joshua. And they've entered Jewish life in another form. In Ashkenazi synagogues, when the reading of one of the five books of the Torah is finished, the congregation calls out: chazak, chazak, venitchazek. Be strong, be strong, and let us be strengthened. When Deuteronomy ends, in two weeks on our path, it will be said again. Courage, in this verse, isn't something Joshua has to find alone. It's given to him, out loud, by the teacher he has served since the early days in the wilderness.
screen: `IN THE SIGHT OF ALL ISRAEL.` · `CHAZAK VE'EMATZ.` · `TWO DOUBTS ANSWERED AT ONCE.` · `CHAZAK, CHAZAK, VENITCHAZEK.` · then, large: `STRONG AND OF GOOD COURAGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: encourage someone publicly. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone stepping into something new or hard. A colleague in a new role, a kid trying out for something, a friend starting over. What do you honestly believe about them? Find one true sentence. Now picture saying it where others can hear it: in a meeting, at the dinner table, in the group chat. Not flattery. Just the true thing, out loud, with your name behind it. The bell holds the time.
Vayelech. And he went. And in it, chazak ve'ematz: be strong and of good courage, said in front of everyone.
Your line: strong and of good courage. Today, encourage one person where others can hear it. Day five hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: When the reading of each of the five books of the Torah is completed, Ashkenazi congregations call out 'chazak, chazak, venitchazek', be strong, be strong, and let us be strengthened; other communities have their own words for the moment.

fork.setup: you're handing your role to Joshua, and the people aren't sure about him. what does Moses do?
options: warn Joshua privately about his weaknesses.
encourage him in front of all Israel.
fork.reveal: a public charge: Joshua hears his teacher's confidence, and the people hear that the role was given, not taken.

original.note: Hebrew: be strong and of good courage. Deuteronomy 31:7.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pep talk.
what it means: public encouragement that gives Joshua confidence, and gives the people confidence in him.
what a scholar hears: the phrase recurs in Deuteronomy 31:6, 7 and 23 and in Joshua 1; 'chazak, chazak, venitchazek' is called out when a book of the Torah is completed.

notes: Deuteronomy 31:7 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory (the verse continues 'for thou shalt go with this people...'); verify punctuation.
'In two weeks on our path': Deuteronomy's end falls on day 536/537 of this path.
Custom of 'chazak, chazak, venitchazek' is Ashkenazi and widespread; some Sephardi communities use a different formula. Keeper may wish to note.
